author: Justin Lundy
title: Greensboro police launch traffic safety campaign after increase in traffic-related deaths - NewsBreak
text:
By Justin Lundy ,
1 hours ago GREENSBORO, N.C. (WGHP) — A troubling trend is taking place on Greensboro streets.
Police say traffic-related deaths are up more than 40% from this time last year. 25 people have been killed so far in 2026.
Greensboro autism facility permanently closes; bankruptcy filing reveals six figure debt As the busy summer months get underway, Greensboro police are rolling out a new enforcement campaign they hope can save lives.
Greensboro Police Officer Wade Crouse says he’s all too familiar with where vehicle crashes often occur.
“I-40 and U.S. 29 or ‘Death Valley.’ There’s a lot of crashes through there, typically multiple throughout the day,” Crouse said.
As a member of the Traffic Safety Unit, one alarming statistic has put him on high alert.
“We’re at 25 [traffic-related deaths] right now, which is a 41% increase over the same time from last year,” Crouse said.
He says there were more than 30 traffic-related deaths in the entirety of 2025.
In 2026, he says the most common cause of traffic-related deaths has been speeding.
“The excessive speed is typically the number one factor in that. But within, you’ve got people failing to yield to right of way, one way or another. Impaired driving has been the root cause several times,” Crouse said,
To reduce the number of vehicle crashes, injuries and deaths, Crouse says GPD is kicking off its newest traffic safety campaign, called ‘Warmer Days. Safer Roadways.
“So we’re not going out randomly and just picking spots and wherever. We’re using data from high-crash locations and fatalities and going out and targeting those areas where those crashes have occurred to encourage voluntary compliance, encourage people to obey the law, drive the speed limit in order to trend down the number of crashes and fatalities,” Crouse said.
As the campaign began, Crouse gave simple but potentially life-saving advice.
“Click it or ticket,” Crouse said. “It’s the easiest thing you can do and make a big difference. A lot of people are unfortunately losing their lives because they aren’t taking the one second it takes to click it. There are seemingly survivable crashes that people are dying in just because they get ejected or being thrown around inside the car where they otherwise may have survived.”
